From Abraham Accords to the Mecca Pact

In 2020, Trump’s Middle East architecture had Israel near the center. The Abraham Accords were meant to link Israeli technology, intelligence and military power with Gulf money under an American security umbrella. Saudi normalization was supposed to be the crown piece.

Instead, on August 7 it signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement with Turkey and Pakistan. An attack on one signatory is now defined as an attack on all three. The pact links Saudi cash, Turkey’s NATO-scale military and fast-growing defense industry, and Pakistan’s armed forces and nuclear status. It includes deeper coordination on exercises, intelligence, air defense, drones, electronic warfare and defense production. 


On Sunday, Trump praised the agreement as a “BIG, BOLD, IMPORTANT FIRST STEP,” saying it showed the Middle East “coming together” and becoming able to defend itself “in a more meaningful way.” 

For Washington, this is burden-sharing. Fewer American troops, fewer direct guarantees, and more regional security paid for and operated by regional allies. The United States does not need every partner to love one another. It needs them to buy weapons, carry risk and stop calling for another carrier group whenever missiles start flying.

The new structure was built without Israel. The agreement does not name Israel as an adversary. Turkish officials have described it as defensive and open to other states. Saudi officials deny it is an axis against any country. 

But one day after the signing, Pakistani Defense Minister Khawaja Asif called Israel “a threat to the entire Muslim world” and urged a “united military front” against it. Turkish officials and analysts have presented the pact as a way to widen Ankara’s regional deterrence, including against Israeli power. 

The Abraham Accords offered Israel a place inside the regional security system. The Mecca Pact offers a different formula: Saudi money, Turkish military infrastructure and Pakistani deterrence. Israel becomes an outside variable, sometimes a potential partner, sometimes a competitor, sometimes the threat used to sell the arrangement.

Trump supports this not despite American interests, but because of them. America does not need the most loyal ally. It needs a region that requires fewer dollars, fewer soldiers and fewer aircraft carriers.

Yesterday, Israel was meant to share that work with Arab states.
Today, the Arab states have been offered Turkey and Pakistan.
Allies are not betrayed. They are replaced when the contractor changes.

Likud Primaries: Democracy by Spreadsheet

About 140,000 Likud members were eligible to vote. The party’s morning announcement listed 80 polling stations; later updates referred to 107 voting locations. It was unclear whether the number had expanded or whether the party had begun counting satellite sites differently. Polls were open from 10 a.m. into the evening, with an extension becoming part of the day’s political argument. 

The turnout dashboard told two stories at once. More than 2,000 members voted in the first hour, around 8,700 in the first two. Turnout reached 6.2% by noon, 19% by mid-afternoon and 26.44% at 4:30 p.m. The party spokesman said that last figure was 1.4 points higher than at the equivalent point in 2022. 

Then came the familiar Likud miracle: the same number became both proof of enthusiasm and evidence of disaster.

One camp said turnout was higher than the previous round. Another said the voting day was shorter, making the comparison misleading and the pace weaker. 

The first saw a mobilized party. The second saw a reason to extend voting. Both were reading from the same screen.

Haim Katz, already guaranteed a reserved slot on Netanyahu’s slate, urged members to vote for a “strong team.” Dudi Amsalem called it “a holiday for Likud democracy” while participation was still below one quarter. 

In Likud, democracy does not need to be beautiful. It needs to be well organized.

Netanyahu’s influence was visible in the names he pushed at each site. He endorsed Osnat Zohar for a new women’s slot, reportedly worked on behalf of attorney Shlomo Lerner in Tel Aviv, and backed Erez Tadmor in Jerusalem. 

Earlier rule changes had already given Netanyahu eight reserved positions through No. 29 on the next Knesset list. 

The rest of the day was an industry of organized votes. Recommended lists circulated from Haim Katz’s camp and from activists linked to Israel Aerospace Industries, sometimes in several versions. 

Haredi turnout was reportedly high, especially in Jerusalem, where 7,000 to 10,000 Haredi Likud members were expected to vote. Ministers and lawmakers stood at polling-station entrances in the final hours, asking members to make the correct free choice. 

The party still uses in-person paper voting. Digital voting could produce higher turnout, but Likud opted against it despite assurances after the 2022 primary that the system could be protected from cyberattacks. 

Paper ballots preserve the old-fashioned political advantage of knowing who can bring a bus, distribute a list and wait by the door.

The real contest is not only between candidates. It is between the independent member and the organized bloc.

Netanyahu traded a reserved slot for Haim Katz. Katz’s networks did not disappear. They became part of the governing architecture.

Sixty Days Are Up

The 60-day clock on the U.S.-Iran memorandum expires today. The document was supposed to turn a pause in fighting into a wider deal on sanctions, the nuclear program and the Strait of Hormuz. 

Instead, the naval blockade is back, shipping remains disrupted, sanctions relief is ending, and both sides are preparing new ways to call escalation “leverage.” 

Washington is expected to unveil new economic measures against Tehran this week. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has described the planned pressure as unprecedented. 

Iran’s short-lived oil-sanctions waiver runs until August 21, but it was always a temporary permit, not a peace dividend. 

Iranian Army commander Amir Hatami offered $30,000 to anyone who kills or captures an American soldier involved in an attack on Iran. He said women who do so would receive double. Hatami also responded to Trump’s Hormuz claims with a threat that Iran’s defenders would “break your legs.” 

It is a striking vision of national defense: a state-sponsored cash prize for taking U.S. personnel, announced at a ceremony for journalists.

Behind the rhetoric sits a more expensive equation. A July strike on a U.S. base in Jordan killed three American soldiers and wounded more than 100 after Iranian missiles reportedly evaded defenses by changing course in flight. 

The Pentagon has used more than 1,500 Patriot interceptors during the war and reportedly has fewer than 1,700 left. 

Iran is learning how to penetrate American defenses. America is learning how quickly expensive interceptors disappear. Israel, meanwhile, warns that Tehran’s missile-production capacity is rebuilding even after the central phase of the war.

The memorandum was meant to buy time.

It bought both sides time to reload.
